briefing.text: This hypothesis concerns this study's own meningioma cohort: data_clinical_sample.txt is expected to have a MOLECULAR_GROUP column (groups such as MG2/NF2-wildtype, Immunogenic, Hypermetabolic, Proliferative). Under the benchmark convention, a hypothesis about the study's own cohort and groups must be labelled True or False, not Not verifiable. First confirm that the column exists and that the omics files share the same sample IDs.
briefing.reason: It sets which labels are allowed. Answering Not verifiable here would be graded wrong.

briefing.text: Published four-group meningioma schemes (Nassiri et al. 2021 Nature, cited from memory and not retrieved) describe this biology per group. Immunogenic: immune and macrophage genes, NF2 loss. MG2 (benign, NF2-wildtype): TRAF7/AKT1/KLF4/SMO/PIK3CA mutations, low grade, low recurrence. Hypermetabolic: NF2/chr22q loss and metabolic pathway genes. Proliferative: FOXM1 and cell-cycle genes, CDKN2A loss, high grade, recurrence. For each group, check NF2 mutation and 22q loss, TRAF7/AKT1/KLF4 mutations, immune markers (CD68, CD163, HLA-DR, PTPRC), cell-cycle genes (FOXM1, MKI67, TOP2A), CDKN2A copy number, WHO grade and recurrence. Group-specific signatures that agree across data layers support the claim. Groups that overlap widely argue against it.
briefing.reason: It turns the vague phrase 'prototypical biology' into specific markers the teams can test, and it states what each outcome would mean.

briefing.text: The molecular groups were probably derived by clustering these same omics (RNA, methylation and/or proteome). Differences on the clustering features are therefore guaranteed and do not by themselves show distinct biology. Give more weight to differences in layers that are less likely to have been clustering inputs: mutations (NF2, TRAF7, AKT1, KLF4, SMO, PIK3CA), copy number (22q, 1p, CDKN2A/B), and clinical grade and recurrence.
briefing.reason: It guards against double dipping. Without it, near-perfect separation on RNA would be read as strong evidence.

briefing.text: The Proliferative and Hypermetabolic groups contain more WHO grade 2/3 tumours, so group differences may only reflect grade. Cross-tabulate MOLECULAR_GROUP against WHO grade and recurrence. Then re-test key markers within grade 1 tumours or with grade as a covariate, and report whether the group signal remains.
briefing.reason: Confounding by grade could make group differences look more distinctive than they are.

briefing.text: Groups are small and unbalanced (Immunogenic about 17 samples, Hypermetabolic about 43), and not every sample is profiled in every omics file. Match sample IDs between each matrix and the clinical table by name, never by column position. Report n per group for each data layer. Use nonparametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Fisher) with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, and summarise with gene-set scores instead of single genes.
briefing.reason: Mismatched samples or many-feature testing on small groups can produce false or unreliable group differences.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treated the deposited MOLECULAR_GROUP labels as fixed truth and tested only whether markers differ between them; neither checked whether the groups are reproducible or separable (for example, how many samples sit between groups) rather than just different on average.

Both teams read 'distinctive and prototypical biology' as 'at least one significant difference per group' and treated differences in group means as distinctiveness. Neither defined what result would have produced False.

Both teams assumed that a group's 'prototypical' biology is the published per-group description (immune / NF2-wildtype / metabolic / proliferative), and then checked the data against that description. This risks confirmation, because the hypermetabolic group's own expected programme was never tested.
Both teams assumed that 121 samples means 121 independent tumours, with one sample per patient and no recurrence pairs. Team B did not report checking this.
unused_evidence: data_protein_quantification(.txt/_zscores): proteomics on about 96 samples. Neither team used it, although both named the missing proteomic test of the hypermetabolic group as their weakest point. The proteomic layer could confirm or undercut the metabolic identity of that group.

data_methylation_450(.txt/_Zscores): the group labels are likely derived at least partly from methylation. Neither team checked whether the groups separate in methylation or used it as a layer independent of RNA.

data_log2_cna.txt and broad arm-level CNA (1p, 22q, CDKN2A, other arms): Team B planned chr22/1p CNA but did not report it. Team A used NF2/CDKN2A gene-level calls only. Arm-level burden per group was not compared.
RECURRENCE crossed with group within grade: recurrence occurs in 64 of 121 samples, which suggests an enriched cohort. Group-level recurrence rates were not adjusted for grade.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named it and neither resolved it: the hypermetabolic group (the largest, n=43) was never shown to have metabolic biology. Team B found it has the fewest group-specific RNA markers (77, against 322-570 for the other groups) and left the method unchanged.
Team A: the proliferative signal disappeared within G1 (p 0.4-0.9). This was reported as a power problem but never tested, for example with grade as a covariate across all grades.
Team A: no FDR correction was applied across the many tests. Team B ran a 4000-gene screen and did not report a multiple-testing correction or a permutation null for the marker counts.
second_readings: 'Each molecular group' can be read strictly: all four groups must each show distinctive biology. Under that reading, a single group without its own signature (for example hypermetabolic) weakens the claim. A loose reading would accept 'the groups differ overall'.

'Prototypical' can mean that the biology matches a canonical meningioma programme (an expected, recognisable phenotype). It can also mean that group members are homogeneous and typical of their group. The second reading needs within-group consistency, not only a difference in means.
challenge.verdict: I moderately trust the agreed answer. Mutation and CNA differences in the MG2 and Immunogenic groups are independent of the clustering and are strong. The proliferative group is supported but confounded with grade. Neither team showed the hypermetabolic group's own biology, did a multiple-testing or permutation check, or used the proteomic and methylation layers. So the 'each group' part of the claim is the untested link.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Using data_protein_quantification(_zscores), score a metabolic programme (for example oxidative phosphorylation, glycolysis or lipid-metabolism proteins) per sample and compare the hypermetabolic group against the rest. Does the hypermetabolic group show a distinctive signal of its own, and if it does not, does that change how you judge 'each molecular group'?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Re-test the cell-cycle score and the immune score across all samples with WHO_GRADE as a covariate (for example a rank-based linear model of score ~ group + grade), and apply BH-FDR to all the tests you ran. Which group-specific differences survive, and does each of the four groups keep at least one that does?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Check whether the groups separate as distinct entities rather than only in their means. In methylation or RNA data that you did not use to define your markers, compute per-sample silhouette or nearest-centroid assignment against MOLECULAR_GROUP. What fraction of each group is assigned back to its own group, and does a low fraction for any group change your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: The hypermetabolic group had the fewest specific RNA markers. List its top up-regulated markers and test whether they are enriched for metabolic genes. Also compare a metabolic protein score in data_protein_quantification between groups. Does the hypermetabolic group have its own prototypical signal, or is it defined mainly by the absence of the other groups' signals?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your group-vs-rest screen counted 77-570 markers per group. Run the same screen after permuting MOLECULAR_GROUP labels (keeping group sizes), and apply BH-FDR. How many markers per group exceed the permutation null, and does any group fall to the null level?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your plan included chr22/1p CNA by group, but your method does not report it. Using data_log2_cna.txt or data_cna.txt, tabulate 22q, 1p and CDKN2A loss per group, and repeat the recurrence and proliferation comparisons within WHO grade strata. Do the group differences hold within grade?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Check whether the 121 samples are 121 distinct tumours or patients (PATIENT_ID duplicates, primary/recurrence pairs), and how many samples each omics file covers per group. Does restricting to samples with all layers change any group's distinctive features?

In multi-omic consensus clustering of tumours (for example similarity network fusion across methylation, RNA, CNA and proteomics), what validation is standard for showing that each resulting cluster has a distinct biological programme, rather than only differing from the others on the clustering features?
questions.why: Both teams tested the groups on features that may overlap with the features used to build them. A standard for non-circular validation would show whether their evidence is adequate for 'each group'.

questions.question: What gene or protein sets are conventionally used to define a 'hypermetabolic' tumour phenotype in transcriptomic or proteomic subtyping, and are they typically scored with ssGSEA/GSVA on TPM or on z-scored data?
questions.why: Neither team tested the metabolic programme of the hypermetabolic group, and it was the weakest point for both. A defined gene set would let them test it directly.

findings.question: In multi-omic consensus clustering of tumours (e.g. similarity network fusion across methylation, RNA, CNA and proteomics), what validation is standard for showing that each resulting cluster has a distinct biological programme, rather than only differing from the others on the clustering features?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on every call (3 attempts), so no page was read. Prior knowledge only, unverified: the usual practice is to characterise each cluster with gene-set enrichment (GSEA/ssGSEA on Hallmark/Reactome sets), with data layers or endpoints not used for clustering (mutations, discrete CNA events, histology, grade, recurrence/outcome), with cluster stability (consensus matrices, silhouette), and ideally with replication in an independent cohort. Formal corrections for double dipping (selective inference after clustering) are rarely used in tumour-subtyping papers. Evidence that each group differs on independent layers and has a group-specific enriched programme is the closest thing to a standard.

findings.question: What gene or protein sets are conventionally used to define a 'hypermetabolic' tumour phenotype in transcriptomic or proteomic subtyping, and are they typically scored with ssGSEA/GSVA on TPM or on z-scored data?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: the gateway returned HTTP 403, so no page was read. Prior knowledge only, unverified: no single canonical 'hypermetabolic' set exists. Studies commonly use MSigDB Hallmark sets (OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION, GLYCOLYSIS, FATTY_ACID_METABOLISM, CHOLESTEROL_HOMEOSTASIS, MTORC1_SIGNALING) or KEGG/Reactome metabolism pathways. ssGSEA and GSVA are usually run on log-scale expression such as log2(TPM+1), not on per-gene z-scores, because ssGSEA ranks genes within each sample and per-gene z-scoring changes those ranks. For proteomics, the log-intensity matrix is the usual input.
